A Desperado Lynched.

Near Belgreene, Ala., Theodore Burton, while splitting rails, got into a feud with John Rockard, whom he killed with two blows of the axe. He fled, but was captured by Eugene Dobbs, James and William Dempsey and Mr. Bushfield. While taking the man back the party stopped to rest. The prisoner suddenly drew his bowie-knife and severely wounded two of his captors and again fled. He was recaptured and placed in jail. At night fifty masked men entered the town and compelled the sheriff to give up the keys of the jail. They then placed the murderer on a horse and quietly rode away. Next morning his body was found hanging to a tree three-quarters of a mile south of the town.

The Northwest Indian Troubles. National Associated Press. Ottawa, Ont., February 23.—There are further rumors of trouble with Indians near Edmonton, where Indians have been raiding a cattle ranch. News has just been received that Indians are rising in Canada northwest, and have destroyed considerable property and several lives. The news is not officially confirmed. Ottawa, February 23.—Mr. Baunnerman, M. P., received a telegram last night from Fort Edmonton, N. W. T., to the effect that that place had been mobbed and the Hudson Bay company's buildings destroyed. The government telegraphed for further particulars, but has received no reply, as the telegraph lines are down west of Winnipeg. BOHANAN'S BREAK. Reappearance of an Old Nebraska Convict. IDENTITY OF THE WAVERLY MURDERER.

LINCOLN, Neb., February 23.—The discovery has been made that Ralvin, who is in the county jail for the murder of James Cook at Waverly Sunday night, is none other than the notorious Quin Bohanan, a former inmate of the penitentiary and a desperado whose name was once a terror along the Missouri river. While an inmate of the penitentiary Quin Bohanan and a man by the name of McWaters headed a revolt which was not quelled until the United States troops were called out and the prison surrounded. The mutiny lasted three days. Bohanan and McWaters took an active part in the revolt, showing unusual courage and nerve. McWaters was afterwards shot dead by a guard. Bohanan served out his time, and was discharged, since which time he has not been seen hereabouts until he appeared as the chief actor in the fiendish murder of Sunday night. Ralvin was arraigned for murder.

MISCELLANEOUS CRIME

COUNTERFEITER CAPTURED.
MILWAUKEE, February 23.—Sam J. Whittaker, the man credited with making and circulating nearly all of the counterfeit eoin in Wisconsin, was captured yesterday near Green Bay and brought to this city.
MURDERER LYNCHED.

MURDERER LYNCHED.

Montgomery, Ala., February 23. Near Bellegreen, Q. H. Barton, while spliting rails, got into a feud with John Rookard and with two blows of an axe killed him and fled. He was captured by Eugene Dobbs, James and Wm. Dempy and Mr. Bushfield. While taking him back the party stopped to rest, when the prisoner suddenly drew a bowie knife and badly wounded two of his captors and fled. He was again recaptured and placed in jail. At night fifty masked men entered the town and going to the sheriff's house demanded the keys of the jail and cage in which the prisoner was confined. After getting possession of them they proceeded to the jail, entered and took the prisoner out, placed him on a horse and rode quietly away. They carried him three-fourths of a mile south and there hung him to a tree. The body was found in the morning.

A YOUTHFUL TRAIN WRECKER.

Dover, N. H., February 23.—Arthur Hunter, 16 years of age, was today committed in default of $10,000 bail for trial for attempting to throw a passenger train off the track of the Denver & Winnapisco railroad by tying a log to the rails over a culvert near Durham. The train was moving slowly at the time and broke the log's fastenings, else it would have been a terrible wreck and loss of life. The boy was found sitting on the fence waiting to see the smash-up. He had heard of the Cole's Crossing disaster and wishing to see one himself.

TRIAL OF TRAIN WRECKERS.

Youngstown, February 23.—On the night of September 28, 1881, a fast line train was thrown from the track of the Pittsburg, Fort Wayne & Chicago railroad near Alliance, O. The train was speeding at the rate of forty miles an hour and dashed into a freight train that had been laid out on a side track. Tehan, engineer, and Wm. Robertson, fireman, of Pittsburg, met with a sudden and horrible death. Detective Johnson, Pinkerton's agency, arrested Nathaniel Lewis, Emanuel Evans, John Lewis and John Shaughnessy December 31, 1881, for the same. The grand jury of this county found indictments of murder against them. John Lewis in the meantime turning state's evidence. The trial began to-day. The first venue was exhausted this evening and another ordered for to-morrow, when court adjourned. The evidence against the accused is strong. It is claimed the murder of the two men was caused by the alleged perpetrators, who claimed bad usage by the railroad company while employed by it.

CONVICT OF CRIMINAL LIBEL.

WASHINGTON, D. C., February 23. Lacy and Bruce, colored editors of the Sunday Item, were to-day convicted of criminal libel against E. P. Howland and M. Mason, dentists.

ESCAPED CONVICT CAPTURED.

CHICAGO, February 23.—John Dougherty, an escaped convict from Lawrence, Mass., was captured to-day and will be taken back to Massachusetts.

SUIT COMPROMISED.

CINCINNATTI, February 23.—Suit against the bondsmen of Ambrose, defaulting ex-United States court clerk for $43,000, has been compromised by the bondsmen paying $15,000.

RETROTING HIS CONFESSION.

LEXINGTON, Ky., February 23.—George W. Ellis, whose confession led

to the conviction of himself, Craft and Neal, as perpetrators of the Ashland tragedy, repudiates his whole statement and claims he is innocent and Craft and Neal had nothing to do with it. He says he was drunk when he made the charge and was compelled to adhere to it on peril of his life

WILL CERTAINLY HANG.

CINCINNATI, February 23.—Major Hicks, the negro convicted of the murder of Williams in Ludlow, Ky., will certainly hang in Covington tomorrow. The gallows is erected in the old work house, and the execution takes place in the presence only of officers and reporters.

THE FAMOUS EXTRADITION CASE.

TORONTO, February 23.—In the J. R. Miller extradition case, judgment was reserved until to-morrow. The result of Mr. Murphy's visit to Ottawa was satisfactory, and it is not likely the prisoner will leave Canada, except under the guarantee that he will be tried only for the offense for which he may be extradited. Mr. Murphy received a telegram from Mr. Hill, who instituted the proceedings, saying that Mr. Connors had been deceived, and that the only true affidavit is that presented by Detective Kribbs, which Judge McKenzie would not recognize. From this, it is apparent that Miller will have to return to Canada in the event of his extradition. Miller himself says he had nothing to do with the robbery.

A WINSTON TRAIN ROBBER SENT UP.

KANSAS CITY, February 23.—Some ten days ago Police Commissioner Craig, accompanied by Sheriff Timberlake of Clay county, went to Adairsville, Ky., and arrested one Jesse Hite, who was living with his father on a farm one and a half miles from that place. He was brought here in irons and lodged in jail. Ever since he has been known as the "mysterious prisoner." The officers would give no information concerning him nor would the prisoner say a word to any reporter. Night before last he was taken to Gallatin, Daviess county, where it appears indictments had been found against him for participating in the Winston train robbery, where Conductor Westfall was killed. Yesterday morning Hite was arraigned in court when he entered a plea of guilty of robbery and was at once sentenced to twenty-five years in the penitentiary. This morning he passed through here in charge of the sheriff of Daviess county, and by the afternoon was in the penitentiary and in convict's garb. It is known that Hite also participated in the Blue Cut train robbery on the Chicago & Alton road a short time after the Winston robbery. He is a cousin of the James boys, and has a brother, Woolson Hite, who is a member of the gang. Jesse Hite is but 23 years of age, and it is believed only became a train robber last summer. At Hockberry, Arizona, a desperado named J. O. Wildon, who had killed John Bullock, was taken from the jail, on the 25th ult., by fifteen men, and hanged to the beam of a blacksmith shop.

D. J. Murphy, formerly district attorney at San Francisco, was shot through the neck, in the police court, on the 25th ult., by Policeman John Morony, who had been referred to as an Australian convict. The latter attempted to kill himself while being taken to prison.

Three masked men entered the farmhouse of Wm. Studebaker, twelve miles from Council and robbed him of $8. Maddened by his obstinacy about surrendering his money, one of the villains shot him through the lungs, inflicting a fatal wound.

Two sheriffs from southern Iowa, armed with a requisition from Gov. Rusk, sought to arrest two robbers at Randolph, Wis. Sberiff Farrell was shot four times, and Wm. Norris received fatal injuries.

J. W. Norris, postmaster and a leading merchant at Rice, Texas, was called out of his house by two men, on the night of the 22d, who asked him to go to his store and sell them some goods. He returned in a few minutes and told his wife that the men had shot him. He died immediately.

Near Belgreene, Ala., on the 23d, John Packard was killed by T. H. Burton, while both were splitting rails. The murderer escaped, but was pursued and captured by three citizens. While taking him back the prisoner badly wounded one of his captors while attempting to escape. He was finally jailed, but at night a band of masked, men took the prisoner from the jail and hung him.

George H. Richardson, of Charlton, Mass., has confessed the murder of his father. The belief was general that Mr. Richardson had been killed by the accidental discharge of a gun while riding in a sleigh with his son. The prisoner claims to have committed the deed to save his mother from abuse.

A man named McAffee, living near Richland, Ark., forced his stepdaughter, aged about 15 years, to occupy his bed, and his wife and the mother of the girl beat his brains out with a gun-barrel.

A mysterious case is now in the hands of the Chicago police. On the 22d a clerk in a music store named J. W. Evans reported at a police station that he had been assaulted in the outskirts of the city and had shot his acquaintance.
Chicago police. On the 22d a clerk in a music store named J. W. Evans reported at a police station that he had been assaulted in the outskirts of the city and had shot his assailant. A search was made and the body of James McNamara, a railroad yard-master, was found. As the deceased was a respected and peaceful citizen, the authorities doubt Evans' story and hold him under arrest.

R. D. Raven and James Cook disputed about the spelling of a word at Lincoln, Neb., on the night of the 20th. Words led to blows, when Raven drew a pistol and shot his opponent dead.

Maxime Potter and brother, with two Americans, all ranchmen, were murdered by Indians in the far northwest, recently.

Two neighbors named Charles Colbetts and Charles Cannon quarrelled about a cow at Deerfield, Mich., on the 20th. The latter was mortally shot by Colbetts, who fled.

John Wyatt, the famous ex-United States Marshall who has bagged more moonshiners than any man in the country was fatally shot at Louisville, Ky., on the 20th, by Jesse Cunningham and Thos. J. Connell, two deputies of the city court.

A grain buyer named James Cook was murdered at Waverly, Neb., on the 19th inst., by a tramp painter named Dick Rayner.
